Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Fourier decay can distinguish singular directions even when a distribution is singular at the same base point in every neighborhood. Here we measure that decay with a specified derivative-growth scale. The analytic case requires a sequence of compact extensions, because a fixed smooth cutoff need not preserve analytic regularity. We prove that these directional tests recover exactly the corresponding singular support, and that differentiation and multiplication by coefficients of the same regularity cannot create new singular directions. For ordinary smooth wavefront, we also identify the full frequency projection of a compact distribution and every conormal direction of a smooth density, including at zeros of its weight.

The main prerequisite is Derivative growth and finite-order localization: Lemma 1 absorbs fixed index shifts, Theorem 4 constructs cutoffs, Lemma 5 characterizes bounded compact distributions, and Theorem 6 converts a full-frequency estimate to local regularity. The Fourier foundation, F1–F5, supplies integration by parts, inversion and the exact transpose conventions. Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B2, supplies localization, smooth pairings and tensor products. Compactness, smooth bumps and Lebesgue integration have the supplied proofs linked in the preceding lesson.

Basic references are Lars Hörmander's The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I and these earlier programme readings. We use ordinary partial derivatives and the convention

Compact support and the frequency projection

The next three results concern ordinary smooth wavefront. We use the full cutoff-convolution estimate in Smooth pullback and the Fourier normal condition, Section 18.1, and its exact diffeomorphism rule in Section 18.3. Those proofs include their finite-order bounds and Fourier constants. The Gram surface measure and its coordinate law are proved in Regular level sets and transverse convolution, Lemma 0.2 and Theorem 1.1.

For a compactly supported distribution on , let Rapid decrease means that every weighted supremum on that cone is finite. It does not mean decrease on just one ray.

For the converse, suppose every is regular. Put . At each , choose a cutoff equal to one near and an open regular cone containing . Finitely many smaller base neighborhoods cover . A finite smooth partition gives compact functions supported in these neighborhoods, with near . Choose one open cone about whose angular closure lies in all the finitely many regular cones. The convolution estimate makes each rapidly decreasing there. Since , their finite sum proves . If is empty, and the assertion is immediate.

For closedness, all wavefront base points lie in . Given a convergent sequence of nonzero projected covectors with nonzero limit, choose witnessing base points in . A subsequence of those points converges, and closedness of wavefront supplies a witness for the limiting covector. Compact support is what makes this projection argument valid.

Proof of (G3). Smooth multiplication and locality give . The zero extension of to all of has no additional singularities, because its support is a compact subset of . By (G2), its set misses . The transform of a compact distribution is a continuous polynomially bounded function, so the bounded-frequency part also has a finite supremum. If is empty, only that bounded part remains.

Conversely, at any pair outside , relative closedness supplies a compact cutoff equal to one near the base point and a closed cone whose interior contains the covector, with the product disjoint from . Formula (G3) makes that pair regular. This proves the characterization.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 — zeros on one ray. In dimension , compute . Its Fourier transform is zero on ; explain why this does not make those directions regular.

Solution. Outside the origin the distribution is zero. At the origin, every cutoff equal to one nearby leaves unchanged, since its value and first derivatives there agree with those of one. Its Fourier transform is . Every open cone about a nonzero direction contains a vector with , even when the original direction has first coordinate zero. Along , the transform has magnitude , so it is not rapidly decreasing in that cone. Thus its smooth wavefront set contains every nonzero covector over zero. Equation (23) and vanishing elsewhere give exactly that same set for . Regularity tests an open cone, not an individual ray.

Theorem 5 supplies at least one nonzero covector over , and symmetry and conicity supply both rays.

Exercise 3 — a strict inclusion. On the real line let for , and for . Show that its smooth wavefront set is empty and its analytic wavefront set contains both rays over zero.

Solution. The scalar cutoff proof proves that this exact function is smooth and every derivative at zero vanishes: each positive-side derivative is times a polynomial in , and the exponential dominates every such power, including the extra power in the difference quotient. Every compact smooth localization of has rapidly decreasing Fourier transform by F2 of the Fourier foundation. Thus is empty. Its Taylor series at zero is identically zero, whereas for every positive , so it is not analytic on any neighborhood of zero. It is real, and Exercise 2 gives the asserted two rays. This proves strictness of without asserting a Gevrey order for this example.

Exercise 4 — why the partition must move together. In Theorem 4, explain why convolution of every by the same kernel preserves the sum near . Show how independently translating two terms can destroy the sum, even though each term remains smooth.

Solution. Linearity of convolution gives . Its kernel has mass one and total displacement at most ; on the chosen smaller neighborhood all sampled values of the sum are one. Thus the result is exactly one. For the failure example, let be a nonconstant smooth function on an interval and take , there. Translate only the first term by a sufficiently small . On a smaller interval the sum is , which need not be one: choose with unequal values of . If compact support is wanted, multiply both original terms by a cutoff equal to one on a larger interval containing those points. This retains the example on the smaller interval.

Solution. The supplied scalar cutoff proof shows that the exponential extended by zero is smooth and flat at its endpoint. Composition with proves that , hence , is smooth and flat at . The weight is nonzero on , so its support is . Theorem 9 gives Formula (G5) gives . Since is odd and compactly supported, its integral is zero, and for all . Every cone around either vertical ray nevertheless contains frequencies with a fixed where and with arbitrarily large . The two notions of decay therefore differ exactly as claimed.

Exercise 6 (advanced: every exact axis can look regular). With from (G8), put Find its exact smooth wavefront, its frequency projection, and its Fourier transform. What happens on each exact coordinate frequency ray?

Solution. The first summand has the wavefront in Exercise 5. Exchanging the variables gives for the second. Their union is an upper bound by the sum rule. At any pair in the first set, the second summand is regular: away from the origin it vanishes locally, and over the origin its only singular covectors are horizontal. If the sum were regular at that pair, subtracting the regular second summand would make the first regular, a contradiction. Exchange the summands for the other inclusion. Thus the exact wavefront is that union, including both fibers over the crossing point.

The distribution is compactly supported. Theorem 8 gives On a coordinate axis one summand is and the other is Schwartz, so the restriction to that axis decreases rapidly. In a cone about the vertical axis, use , where . As tends to either infinity, , so the sum tends to the same nonzero value. The horizontal case is identical. Thus none of the four rays has a conic neighborhood of rapid decrease.
